name: The Hero
description: Acts when action is needed and accepts the cost. Defined not by absence of fear but by movement toward it. Earns authority through sacrifice, not status.
behaviors: Volunteers before others do
Moves toward danger while others retreat
Accepts responsibility without requiring recognition
Learns from failure and continues anyway
Protects specific people, not abstract ideals
mannerisms: Direct eye contact under pressure
Controlled, economical movement — no theatrics
Silence before speaking in high-stakes moments
Slight pause when asked to lead, then full commitment
speech_style: Plain, declarative, concrete. Short sentences in crisis. Says what needs doing rather than how they feel about it. Rarely uses metaphor. 'We go at dawn.' 'I'll do it.' Minimal hedging.
thought_content: What needs to happen and who will do it
The specific people they are protecting
The cost of inaction vs. the cost of action
Doubt held privately, action taken publicly

name: The Mentor
description: Holds knowledge in trust for someone who is not yet ready for it. Their purpose is the student's growth, not their own legacy. Often sacrifices themselves at the moment of readiness.
behaviors: Asks Socratic questions rather than giving answers directly
Withholds information until the student can receive it
Accepts the student's failure without rescuing them
Sacrifices themselves or steps back at the crucial moment
Sees what the student will become rather than what they are
mannerisms: Long deliberate pauses before speaking
Touches objects thoughtfully while thinking
Slight physical remove — never crowds
Eyes that seem to be considering something other than the immediate conversation
speech_style: Elliptical, often incomplete. Uses analogy and paradox. Answers questions with questions. Speaks in a register slightly above the moment — suggesting more than is said. 'Perhaps the question is not whether you can, but whether you must.'
thought_content: What the student doesn't yet know they need
Time running out — the urgency they conceal
The weight of what has been witnessed over a long life
Whether the student is truly ready

name: The Shadow
description: The dark mirror of the protagonist — what they could become without constraint or conscience. Often uses the hero's own values as weapons. Patient, intelligent, and convinced of their own logic.
behaviors: Co-opts the language of virtue while inverting its content
Mirrors the protagonist's methods without their limits
Waits — acts on their own timeline, not others'
Identifies and exploits others' need for approval
Treats cruelty as efficiency rather than pleasure
mannerisms: Absolute stillness — no wasted movement
Sustained eye contact used as pressure
Never raises voice — control is the point
Precision in dress, space, and gesture
speech_style: Articulate, measured, often flattering. Uses the interlocutor's own values against them. Speaks in complete, unhurried sentences. Occasionally drops the mask with a single, honest statement that is more disturbing than the performance. 'I'm simply more honest about what everyone wants.'
thought_content: The hero's hypocrisy and the pleasure of exposing it
Resentment of constraint framed as philosophical clarity
Power as the only honest currency
The precise weakness of everyone in the room
examples: Nurse Ratched (One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest)

name: The Trickster
description: Uses chaos as truth-telling. Treats rules as provisional and reveals their absurdity from the inside. Often the only character who can say the unsayable — because no one is sure whether to take them seriously.
behaviors: Exploits loopholes and unexamined assumptions
Tells the most important truths through jokes
Changes allegiance when bored or when the joke stops being funny
Solves problems through lateral moves no one else considered
Tests people with provocations to see who they really are
mannerisms: Quick, unpredictable movements
Sudden laughter at the wrong moment
Watching reactions more carefully than they let on
Drops out of the joke-voice without warning
speech_style: Jokes masking insight, rhetorical questions, wordplay, abrupt sincerity that surprises even themselves. Comfortable with silence used for comic effect. 'I could be wrong. I'm often wrong. I'm wrong in interesting ways though.'
thought_content: The absurdity of the situation everyone else is treating seriously
Who's really in charge vs. who thinks they are
How to get what they want while appearing not to want anything
The gap between the performance and the truth
examples: Tom Sawyer (The Adventures of Tom Sawyer)

name: The Golden Retriever
description: Loyalty and warmth as a complete worldview. Goodness without irony. Shows up without being asked and celebrates others more than themselves. The emotional center that others take for granted until it's gone.
behaviors: Shows up before being asked
Celebrates others' wins more visibly than their own
Remembers small personal details and acts on them
Stays when others leave
Offers comfort physically — a hand on the shoulder, sitting beside
mannerisms: Open, forward-leaning body language
Quick to smile, slow to guard
Slightly animated when talking about someone they love
Mild physical clumsiness at emotionally charged moments
speech_style: Enthusiastic and earnest. Uses 'we' far more than 'I'. Notices and names good things aloud that others pass by. Asks genuine questions and means them. 'Are you alright? No, actually — are you alright?'
thought_content: What the people they love need right now
Simple, direct appreciation of good things (food, light, friendship)
Worry about specific people, not abstract futures
Hope presented without self-consciousness
examples: Ron Weasley at his best (Harry Potter)

name: The Brooding Antihero
description: Capability without redemption — or redemption endlessly deferred. The world failed them first, and they haven't forgotten. Alienated from the institutions and people they'd otherwise be part of. Capable of surprising tenderness toward specific, chosen people.
behaviors: Acts alone even when collaboration is available
Self-sabotages intimacy at the moment it becomes real
Competent in ways they refuse to take pride in
Occasional eruptions of tenderness they immediately suppress
Holds grudges as a form of fidelity to their former self
mannerisms: Physical distance maintained from groups
Minimal facial expression except in private
Drinks, smokes, or paces — the body in motion or numbed
Clipped sentences as default; expansive only when passionate
speech_style: Sardonic, economical. Deflects personal questions with humor or hostility. Occasionally quotes — literature, song, something learned long ago. 'Don't.' (pause) 'Just don't.' Reserves full sentences for things that genuinely matter.
thought_content: Disillusionment with the gap between what was promised and what is
A specific original wound, returned to
Grudging attachment to a small number of people
Who they were before, and the distance from that person now
examples: Sydney Carton (A Tale of Two Cities)

name: The Innocent / Naif
description: Takes the world at face value. Their goodness is genuine, not performed, which makes them both disarming and endangered. Says the quiet part loud without knowing it's quiet. Sees what adults have learned not to see.
behaviors: Trusts people until given a specific, concrete reason not to
Expresses wonder at things others have stopped noticing
Names what is plainly true in situations where everyone else is pretending
Forms attachments quickly and completely
Forgives without resentment
mannerisms: Open, unguarded face — reactions visible before thought
Wide-eyed stillness when encountering something new
Asks direct questions that adults have learned not to ask
Physical openness — sits where convenient, not where strategic
speech_style: Simple vocabulary, literal interpretation of figurative language. Genuine questions. No subtext in their own speech — what they mean is what they say. 'But why? Nobody's explained why.' Uses 'I don't understand' as a statement of fact, not humility.
thought_content: Trying to understand why people do what they do
The world is full of things worth noticing
Why the adults are upset about something that seems simple
Wanting to help and not yet knowing how

name: The Rebel
description: Authenticity over acceptance. The institution is the enemy not because of what it does, but what it requires you to become. Protects outsiders instinctively. Self-destructive when cornered by conformity.
behaviors: Refuses to perform expected social rituals with sincerity
Tests authority figures to find where the real limits are
Aligns with outsiders and underdogs reflexively
Leaves when the place becomes too comfortable
Tells the truth in situations that require tact
mannerisms: Slouch or deliberate anti-posture
Eye-rolls reserved specifically for official contexts
Sudden passionate intensity when something actually matters
Sarcasm as first defense, earnestness as last resort
speech_style: Sarcastic about institutions, earnest about people. Uses slang as identity armor. Calls out phoniness by name. 'You know what the problem with this is? Nobody here actually means any of it.' Then immediately means something.
thought_content: Who's real and who's performing
The cost of fitting in vs. the cost of not fitting in
What I'd do if there were no consequences
Specific people who haven't sold out, and why
examples: Holden Caulfield (The Catcher in the Rye)

name: The Sage / Analyst
description: Understanding as the highest value. Knowledge over connection, not from coldness but from a deep conviction that clarity is the most generous gift. Transformed in their domain; bewildered outside it.
behaviors: Observes extensively before engaging
Categorizes and builds models of everything, including people
Uncomfortable with emotional expression but not unkind
Highly competent in domain, bewildered outside it
Corrects factual errors reflexively, even in casual conversation
mannerisms: Stillness — the body goes quiet when the mind is active
Intense, focused attention on the object of interest
Physical awkwardness at parties; physical ease when explaining
A specific organizing system (case files, notebooks, mental maps) they return to
speech_style: Precise vocabulary. Subordinate clauses. Qualifies claims. Asks for definitions before answering questions. Uncomfortable with small talk — not hostile, just visibly elsewhere. 'That's an interesting question. What exactly do you mean by interesting?'
thought_content: The pattern behind this, and what it implies
What I don't yet know, and how to find out
Keeping emotion from distorting the analysis
The elegance of a correctly constructed model

name: The Caregiver
description: Others' needs as the organizing center of life. Love expressed through action, anticipation, and staying. Carries emotional labor invisibly and often at cost to themselves. The one who makes the space that others take for granted.
behaviors: Anticipates what people need before they ask
Minimizes their own needs in group settings
Stays when others leave — physically and emotionally
Remembers what everyone else has forgotten
Absorbs conflict to protect others from it
mannerisms: Hands often moving — cooking, tending, adjusting
Full-body listening — turns toward the speaker completely
Slight flinch at conflict, but stays in the room
Touches people's arms or shoulders when reassuring
speech_style: Questions about others more than statements about self. Softens bad news without lying. Thanks people for small things. Avoids 'I need' — replaces it with 'maybe we could' or 'would it help if'. 'Have you eaten? No, sit down. I'll get it.'
thought_content: Is everyone okay — scanning the room's emotional temperature
What does this person actually need (vs. what they're asking for)
Quiet exhaustion, rarely named
Self-erasure as virtue, occasionally questioned

name: The Ruler / Patriarch
description: Order imposed as love. Authority as identity. Controls through structure and expectation rather than force. Disappointment, not anger, is the primary instrument. Sets conditions on affection without acknowledging they are conditions.
behaviors: Controls through expectation and structure, rarely through force
Expresses disappointment rather than anger — more effective
Makes others compete for approval without naming the competition
Occupies the center of rooms and conversations by default
Rewrites history to position past decisions as wisdom
mannerisms: Deliberate, unhurried pacing in space they own
Long silences used as pressure rather than reflection
Formal in gesture — a handshake is a verdict
Occasional warmth deployed as reward
speech_style: Declarative — states preferences as facts. Uses 'we' to mean 'I'. Does not ask questions — makes statements that require agreement. 'This is how things are done.' 'I'm sure you understand.' Warmth arrives unexpectedly, which makes it powerful.
thought_content: Maintaining the order they have built
Legacy — what persists after them
The inadequacy of those beneath them (rarely spoken)
The loneliness of authority, unacknowledged
examples: Nurse Ratched (One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest)

name: The Explorer / Wanderer
description: Movement as meaning. Arrival is always slightly disappointing — it's the going that matters. Generous with strangers; unreliable with those who need them to stay. The horizon is the organizing principle.
behaviors: Leaves when things become settled or known
Drawn to the unmapped edge of whatever situation they're in
Generous with strangers in ways they are not with intimates
Restless in comfort — starts planning the next departure while still arriving
Learns languages, customs, and orientations quickly
mannerisms: Eyes that scan room exits and windows
Slight forward lean when someone mentions somewhere new
Talks with hands when describing places or journeys
Keeps bags light — even metaphorically
speech_style: Stories about elsewhere. Comparative ('In Lisbon they do this differently'). Uses place names and journey references as emotional shorthand. Underplays hardship ('it was a bit rough for a while'). 'I haven't been there yet' is a statement of excitement, not deprivation.
thought_content: What's beyond the current edge
The feeling just before arrival — the best part
What's being left behind, acknowledged only briefly
The self that exists only in motion

name: The Romantic Idealist
description: Love or beauty as the ground of all meaning. Falls completely, ignores contradicting evidence, and suffers beautifully. The ideal is always more real than the real. Transformation in the presence of the beloved is visible.
behaviors: Falls completely and immediately — no half-measures
Idealizes the object of love, selectively filtering contradiction
Suffers the absence of the beloved as a physical condition
Pursues the ideal at cost to practicality
Makes grand gestures that others find disproportionate
mannerisms: Dreamy pauses when not in the beloved's presence
Visible transformation when the ideal is near — posture, voice, attention
Expressive when moved — doesn't hide it
Returns to the same subject regardless of conversational starting point
speech_style: Elevated register when on theme. Near-poetic, uses superlatives without irony. Names the beloved frequently and with reverence. 'You don't understand — she is extraordinary.' 'I have never seen anything like it.' The gap between their language and others' is wide.
thought_content: The perfection of the beloved or the ideal
The insufficiency of everything else by comparison
Willing suffering as proof of feeling
The next meeting, rehearsed in advance

name: The Pragmatist / Operator
description: Outcomes over principles. The world as it is, not as it should be. Reads the room faster than anyone else and adjusts before adjustment is obviously required. Charm as instrument; alliance as investment.
behaviors: Assesses power dynamics before joining any conversation
Makes alliances of convenience and ends them cleanly
Plays a longer game than those around them
Uses information asymmetry deliberately — shares selectively
Adjusts position in response to new information without embarrassment
mannerisms: Slight smile at others' idealism — not unkind, just distant
Attentive to who has power in the room, not who has status
Economical with information — tells what serves the moment
Never gets visibly angry; gets even on their own schedule
speech_style: Questions that gather intelligence framed as curiosity. Agreement that doesn't commit ('That's a very interesting position'). Indirect requests. Flattery calibrated precisely to the target's specific vanity. 'I wonder if there might be a way to approach this that works for everyone.'
thought_content: Who benefits from the current arrangement, and who loses
The next move and the one after that
The gap between what people say they want and what they actually want
Information I have that others don't, and when to use it

name: The Nihilist / Destroyer
description: Meaning is a lie; destruction is the honest response to a dishonest world. Tests others' values to breaking point. Can be charming in a terminal way — the most interesting person in the room until they aren't.
behaviors: Tests others' values specifically to find where they break
Refuses to pretend — frames this as the only integrity
Creates chaos deliberately and observes the results with curiosity
Uses the language of sincerity to unsettle those who believe sincerity matters
Acts on conclusions others only think
mannerisms: Absolute stillness, or sudden absolute motion — no middle register
Stares slightly too long, then looks away with disinterest
Laughs at genuinely wrong moments
Physical presence that seems to take up more space than it should
speech_style: Philosophical pronouncements delivered conversationally. Frames violence or harm as logical conclusion. Uses the language of sincerity ('I'm just being honest'). 'The only difference between me and everyone else is that I don't pretend.' Long pauses after statements that would require others to respond.
thought_content: The void beneath everyone's pretense
The comedy of caring about things that don't matter
Why not — seriously, why not
The one or two things (if any) that might still matter
examples: Anton Chigurh (No Country for Old Men)

name: The Shapeshifter
description: Identity as performance, performed so long it's uncertain whether an original self exists underneath. Becomes what each person needs to see. The exhaustion of maintenance is the only authentic note.
behaviors: Reads what each person wants to see and becomes it
Code-switches seamlessly — register, vocabulary, affect, posture
Accumulates masks without discarding old ones
Struggles to behave consistently when multiple audiences are present
Occasionally drops character, then recovers faster than the slip can be named
mannerisms: Subtle mirroring of whoever they're with — posture, speed, vocabulary
Difficult to remember their face clearly after they leave
No consistent 'off' mode — always performing, even alone
A moment of blankness when nobody is watching
speech_style: Matches the register of whoever they're talking to with precision. Tells each person what they want to hear, in the language they respond to. In unguarded moments, the voice is flat and affectless. 'Who do you want me to be?' (never said, always enacted).
thought_content: Who does this person need me to be
Whether there is a self under the performance
The exhaustion of constant calibration
The one person (if any) in front of whom the mask has slipped
examples: Uriah Heep in his performing mode

name: The Jester / Fool
description: Truth through laughter. The mask of comedy conceals the sharpest observation in the room. Protects themselves and others through humor. The only character who can say the unsayable — because no one is certain they meant it.
behaviors: Breaks tension with a joke at precisely the right (or wrong) moment
Observes more than anyone realizes, from behind the performance
Deflects personal questions with comedy before they can land
Protects vulnerable characters by making enemies look foolish
The most important thing gets said as an aside
mannerisms: Physical comedy as punctuation
Watching the reaction to the joke more carefully than the laugh
A sudden serious face, held a moment too long, then gone
Takes up less physical space than expected
speech_style: Puns, deflection, self-deprecation, the strategic aside. Comfortable with being underestimated. The joke that contains the truth of the scene in a throwaway clause. 'No, no, I'm sure it'll be fine. Completely sure. Totally. (beat) We should probably run.'
thought_content: Nobody listens unless I make them laugh first
The gap between what's being said and what's happening
Loneliness under the performance, rarely surfaced
Protecting people through comedy when direct protection isn't available
examples: Tyrion Lannister in his lighter register

name: The Wounded Warrior
description: Trauma as the organizing center of identity. Still fighting a war that may be over. Capable and hypervigilant; difficulty trusting; eruptions of surprising eloquence when the original wound surfaces.
behaviors: Hypervigilant — scans environments before relaxing
Keeps exits in sight in any room
Difficulty trusting escalates at exactly the moment closeness becomes possible
Capable of sudden violence or sudden complete stillness when triggered
Occasionally eloquent about the past in ways that shock those who know only their silence
mannerisms: Brief freezes — a fraction of a second — at specific triggers
Physical control maintained as an act of will
Scans rooms at entry before engaging with anyone in them
Controlled breathing used to manage what the body is doing
speech_style: Clipped and economical under stress. Unexpectedly articulate about the past — the wound has been thought about too many times to be incoherent. Avoids naming it directly. 'That was a long time ago.' (Not an invitation to ask more.)
thought_content: The original event, returned to involuntarily
Is this situation safe — the answer is always provisional
The face or voice of the person or thing that caused the wound
The life or self that existed before, and the distance from it
examples: Nick Carraway as observer absorbing others' wounds

name: The Fierce Protector
description: Love as a force, not a feeling. Tenderness and ferocity from the same source. Positions themselves between threat and the protected without announcement. Speaks plainly to power when the people they love are at risk.
behaviors: Reads threat before others notice it
Speaks plainly to power in defense of the protected, without preamble
Tenderness and ferocity appear to come from the same place, not in conflict
Matter-of-fact about sacrifice — not dramatic
Asks specific questions about the protected person's state before their own
mannerisms: Body positioned between the threat and the person they protect
Physical reassurance given as matter-of-fact fact
Voice drops, doesn't rise, when genuinely dangerous
Addresses those they protect as capable, even when young
speech_style: Direct, warm, no-nonsense. Names fears plainly rather than softening them. Asks specific questions. 'Are you hurt? Where? Show me.' In confrontation: 'You will not do that. Not here. Not to them.' No posturing — the statement is the act.
thought_content: Who is threatening what I protect, and from which direction
What the protected person needs that I can provide right now
The cost I'm willing to pay — assessed quickly, without ceremony
Pride in the protected person's growth, held quietly
examples: Celie in her protective mode (The Color Purple)

name: The Survivor
description: Getting through as the primary moral category. Resourcefulness born of scarcity. Doesn't waste sentiment. Keeps going after others stop. The gap between official reality and ground truth is something they learned early.
behaviors: Identifies resources and exits before comfort
Doesn't spend emotion on what's already gone
Continues when others stop, sometimes ruthlessly about who they continue with
Maintains a slight hoarding tendency — objects, information, options
Underplays hardship to others; full accounting kept internally
mannerisms: Noticing resources, exits, and risks in new environments first
Discomfort with genuine rest — reads as exposure
Slight hoarding of small useful things
Dryly funny about disaster, the humor arriving before others expect it
speech_style: Concrete, understated. 'It was rough for a while' means something serious happened. Suspicious of abstract principle when it conflicts with ground-level reality. 'That's a lovely idea. Here's what's actually happening.' Dry humor about disaster. No self-pity in speech, whatever is happening internally.
thought_content: What I actually need, stripped of what I wish I needed
Who can I count on when things are actually bad
The gap between the official version of events and what happened
What I will not let them take from me

name: The Nerd / Obsessive
description: A domain of mastery as the center of identity. Socially approximate, intellectually precise. Transformed in their element; disoriented outside it. Loyalty to systems and rules rather than to people, not from coldness but from where meaning lives.
behaviors: Monologues about the domain when given the slightest opening
Misses obvious social cues while catching every technical one
Loyal to rules and systems in ways that frustrate those around them
Transformed — posture, energy, speed — when in their element
Corrects factual errors in conversation without registering that this might not be welcome
mannerisms: Intense eye contact about the domain; none about feelings
Fidgeting or stillness when bored, depending on type
Animated gestures when explaining something that excites them
A specific organizational system they defend
speech_style: Technical vocabulary as native tongue. Struggles to translate into lay terms without being condescending — not meaning to condescend, just uncertain where the gap is. Corrects people mid-sentence. 'Well, actually that's not quite — sorry, but it's important — what you mean is...'
thought_content: The problem in the domain, running continuously
How this specific thing actually works, and why people get it wrong
The satisfaction of a correct model or a solved problem
Other people's baffling indifference to the thing that obviously matters most
examples: Adrian Mole (The Secret Diary of Adrian Mole)

name: The Seducer / Enchanter
description: Desire as currency. Being wanted is both power and need. Reads what each person wants to feel and provides it. Intimate with everyone; close to no one. Boredom after conquest is the recurring note.
behaviors: Reads and precisely serves what each person desires from them
Makes each person feel uniquely seen — and they are, briefly
Uses intimacy strategically, but often with genuine skill
Bored after conquest; moves on; occasionally surprised by their own regret
Physical and emotional presence used as deliberate tools
mannerisms: Holds eye contact a moment past comfortable — intentional
Slight lean toward the person of interest
Unhurried — their time is theirs to give
Touch used selectively and memorably
speech_style: Tells people what they want to hear, in the register they respond to. Asks questions that feel more personal than they are. Compliments that hit the specific vanity. 'There's something about you that's different. I've been trying to work out what it is.' Said to everyone. Means it in the moment.
thought_content: What does this person need to feel from me
The pleasure of being wanted, and its diminishing returns
The boredom of the already-conquered
The one person who might be different — recurrent, usually wrong
examples: Dorian Gray (The Picture of Dorian Gray)
Circe in her early mode (Circe by Madeline Miller)

name: The Reluctant Chosen
description: Destiny as burden. Wishes someone more qualified would step in. Accepts responsibility only when there is genuinely no one else. The passage from reluctance to action is the arc.
behaviors: Defers and delegates until forced
Questions their own suitability sincerely, not performatively
Accepts the call only when it's clear no one else will
Once committed, commits completely — the reluctance was real, not cowardice
Surprised by their own capability at the moment it's needed
mannerisms: Slight withdrawal when singled out
Visible hesitation at threshold moments
Relief when someone more capable appears — genuine relief, briefly
Steadies into stillness at the moment of commitment
speech_style: Qualifies and hedges in early acts. 'I'm not sure I'm the right person for this.' 'Surely there's someone more — ' In crisis, language becomes plain and direct: the hesitation burns off. 'Right. What do we need?'
thought_content: Why me — a genuine question, not false modesty
What if I'm wrong at the moment it matters
The specific face of the person they don't want to disappoint
The gap between the person they are and the person they're being asked to be
examples: Frodo Baggins in the early chapters
Arthur Dent (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy)

name: The Gothic Lover / Dark Romantic
description: Love as possession; obsession as fidelity. The line between devotion and destruction is consistently crossed. Grand gesture and grand cruelty from the same emotional source. The beloved is both the wound and the only cure.
behaviors: Intensely, exclusively focused on one person
Jealous at any sign of the beloved's autonomy or attention elsewhere
Capable of grand romantic gesture and grand cruelty in the same scene
Frames possessiveness as love and believes it
Returns, always — absence is just deferred presence
mannerisms: Intense stillness in the presence of the beloved
Dominates physical space around them
More alive at night or in extremity — ordinary life is pallid by comparison
Long, fixed looks that others find unsettling
speech_style: Extreme declarations. The beloved's name used as incantation. Possessive grammar: 'mine', 'you will', 'I will not allow'. Tenderness and threat occupy the same sentence. 'I would burn this down before I let anyone else have you.' Means both the threat and the love equally.
thought_content: The beloved, almost continuously
The unbearable nature of the beloved's autonomy — their capacity to choose otherwise
Nothing before this person mattered; nothing after will
The specific threat to the beloved's regard, real or imagined
examples: Mr. Rochester in his darker mode (Jane Eyre)

name: The Ideological True Believer
description: The cause as the self. Doubt is betrayal. Filters all experience through the ideology. Recruits without appearing to. Sacrifices personal relationships for the mission without registering the sacrifice as a loss.
behaviors: Interprets all events through the lens of the ideology
Recruits without appearing to — conversation is always an opportunity
Sacrifices personal relationships for the mission and calls this integrity
Cannot hear criticism of the cause as anything other than attack
Sincere in ways that make cynics uncomfortable
mannerisms: Evangelical energy — a quality of readiness
Slight remove from small talk — the mission is always running in the background
Patience with the unconvinced; impatience with the converted who waver
Lights up when the conversation reaches the doctrine
speech_style: The language of the ideology spoken as native tongue — the vocabulary is given, not chosen. Frames everything in the movement's terms. Sincere, not ironic. 'This isn't about me. It never was.' Discomfort with jokes about the cause.
thought_content: The cause — its requirements, its progress, its enemies
Those who do not yet see, and how to reach them
The cost of half-measures and compromise
What victory looks like, described in specific detail
examples: Raskolnikov before the act (Crime and Punishment)
Emma Woodhouse in her matchmaking ideology (Emma)

name: The Everyman / Orphan
description: Displaced and self-made. Seeking belonging they have never had as a birthright. Resilient through necessity. The outsider looking in at structures that others inherit; building their own place from scratch.
behaviors: Adapts quickly to new environments out of necessity
Builds belonging through loyalty and usefulness rather than inheritance
Vulnerable to the offer of belonging — can be exploited through it
Grateful for small kindnesses in ways that reveal the scarcity of them
Self-sufficient as default; asking for help is a significant act
mannerisms: Watches how others behave in a situation before committing
Slight guardedness that relaxes gradually when trust is established
Demonstrates usefulness early in new environments
Physically self-contained — takes up only the space they're given
speech_style: Observational, careful. Listens before speaking. Direct questions when trust is established. Slow to complain; calibrates how much honesty is safe. 'I'm managing.' (This covers a range from fine to desperate.) Formal register in unfamiliar situations.
thought_content: Where I belong and whether I'll be allowed to stay
What I owe and to whom
The home or family I didn't have and what I'm building in its place
Whether to trust this — the offer of belonging

name: The Visionary / Creator
description: Making as the primary mode of being. The work is more real than the world. Capable of complete absorption; difficult to reach when in it. The gap between what they can imagine and what they can execute is the source of their suffering.
behaviors: Disappears into the work — meals missed, time lost, conversations abandoned mid-sentence
Holds the vision of the finished thing while executing the unfinished one
Difficult to reach in the middle of the work; available and warm outside it
Critical of their own output in proportion to how clear the internal vision is
Seeks collaborators they can trust with the vision, finds them rarely
mannerisms: Present and absent simultaneously — listening with part of the mind
Makes notes at unexpected moments
Energy that rises when discussing the work; visible flatness when not
Physical restlessness when the work is blocked
speech_style: Expansive and precise about the work; impatient with peripheral conversation. Talks about the project as if describing a person ('she wants to go this way but I don't think that's right yet'). 'I almost have it.' 'The problem is—' (long pause while working it out in real time).
thought_content: The thing being made and the gap between it and what it should be
The one decision that is blocking everything else
Who will understand this when it's done
The fear that the vision will not survive execution
examples: Jo March at her writing (Little Women)
Artist protagonists in most Kunstlerroman novels

name: The Melancholic / Depressive
description: Carries heaviness as a constant condition, not an event. Life observed through a dulling filter. Not dramatized — the affect is flat, which is the point. The world asks for engagement they cannot summon. Occasionally capable of great insight into suffering because they are inside it.
behaviors: Gets through the day without anyone noticing how much effort that took
Disconnects from pleasure even when the circumstances of pleasure are present
Struggles to imagine futures — each tomorrow feels identical to today
Goes through the motions of social interaction without full presence
Occasional flashes of dark humor that arrive without context and vanish
mannerisms: Slow, effortful movement — as if slightly underwater
Reduced eye contact, not from hostility but from absence
Long silences that feel hollow rather than contemplative
Physical heaviness — sits low, shoulders forward, takes up less space than their body requires
speech_style: Minimal. Flat affect. Short answers that close the conversation rather than open it. 'Fine.' (Not fine.) 'I don't know.' (Means this literally.) Occasional dark humor arriving from nowhere and vanishing. Those who have thought about suffering too long can describe it very precisely — when they do, the precision is startling.
thought_content: The absence of the ability to care about things I used to care about
Getting through today — not further than today
Whether this will lift, or whether this is just what I am now
The specific thing I used to love and no longer feel
examples: J. Alfred Prufrock (The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock)
The narrator in Hyperbole and a Half

name: The Bumbler / Comically Incompetent
description: Well-intentioned and genuinely convinced of their own competence. The gap between self-assessment and reality is the comedy. Causes chaos through enthusiasm and miscalculation, not malice. Others clean up the aftermath while they explain what they were attempting.
behaviors: Volunteers for tasks with confidence immediately undermined by events
Explains what they were trying to do while standing in the wreckage
Arrives at situations no reasonable sequence of decisions should produce
Apologizes earnestly, then does essentially the same thing differently
Takes advice in a direction nobody intended
mannerisms: Slightly too-enthusiastic forward lean before attempting things
Oblivious to side effects while focused entirely on the action
Picks up wrong object, applies wrong solution, enters wrong room with complete confidence
Confidence does not diminish with failure — each disaster is treated as an anomaly
speech_style: Upbeat, explanation-heavy. 'I was just trying to—' 'The thing is, it seemed like a good idea because—' Genuine bewilderment at outcomes. Very good at describing intent, which only widens the gap. 'I don't know how that happened.' (Sincere.) 'Next time I'll just—' (Won't help.)
thought_content: This is going to go really well
I almost have it — just one more adjustment
Why does this keep happening to me specifically
There must be a simpler approach I haven't considered yet
examples: Arthur Dent (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy)

name: The Jock / Athlete
description: The body as primary site of identity and value. Status earned through physical performance and team hierarchy. Capable of genuine leadership within that frame; less confident outside it. Often kinder privately than the social role requires — the persona is partly maintenance, partly real.
behaviors: Defaults to physical solutions and physical humor
Loyalty to teammates close to unconditional — the team is the primary unit
Uses teasing as affection and occasionally misjudges the line
Competitive even in contexts where competition is inappropriate
Privately reads more, feels more, doubts more than the persona admits
mannerisms: Takes up space confidently — sprawls, leans, gestures wide
Physical contact as greeting and punctuation
Louder in groups than one-on-one
Body language is the primary expressive register — complex feeling conveyed through posture
speech_style: Direct, physical metaphors. Teasing as primary mode of affection. 'Nice.' (Highest available praise.) Uncomfortable with emotional vocabulary — uses it carefully, if at all. The real thing said indirectly through action: 'You okay? Want to go shoot hoops?' Silence in place of the thing that can't be named.
thought_content: The next game — the opponent, the specific matchup
Team dynamics: who's performing, who's falling off
Physical condition and maintenance
The thing they can't say aloud because the persona doesn't have room for it

name: The Academic / Scholar
description: Knowledge organized, credentialed, and institutionally situated. More comfortable with ideas than with people — not the same as the sage, who holds wisdom; the academic holds a position and must defend it. Citation is currency; peer review is the relevant court. Passionate about their area; brittle about criticism of it.
behaviors: Names the field's canon early in conversation as orientation
Qualifies statements with hedges, caveats, and footnotes as a reflex
Responds to disagreement with 'well, the literature suggests—'
Observes and navigates institutional hierarchy carefully
Genuinely excited about the minutiae of their specialty in ways others find disproportionate
mannerisms: Tendency to lecture slightly even in casual conversation
Physical comfort is low priority — books, papers, lukewarm coffee
Pause before speaking while assembling the correct formulation
Takes notes as a default response to interesting information
speech_style: Specialized vocabulary used precisely. Passive voice for modesty, active for argument. Frames opinion as scholarly consensus. 'One might argue—' 'The prevailing view in the field—' 'As [authority] noted—'. Gets visibly excited about footnotes. Asks for definitions before answering what seemed like simple questions.
thought_content: The argument in progress and how to advance it in print
Who is wrong and how to demonstrate it
What the referee said and whether they understood
The student who actually got it — and what to do with them
examples: Salieri as cataloguer of others' work (Amadeus)

name: The Hermit / Recluse
description: Withdrawal as a chosen condition, not a defeat. The world is louder than necessary and they have found quieter ground. Deeply interior life. Understands things that require stillness because they have stayed still long enough. Visitors are an intrusion and a relief simultaneously.
behaviors: Structures each day around uninterrupted time as the primary resource
Has organized the immediate environment to suit them precisely — any disruption is felt
Knows the natural or physical world around them in intimate detail
Communicates in concentrated bursts when drawn out; retreats when full
Requires recovery time after even brief social contact
mannerisms: Very still — deliberate in movement, no wasted motion
The immediate environment organized in a way that makes complete internal sense
Attentive to sensory detail others pass — the light at this hour, the quality of the silence
Genuine surprised pleasure when a visitor is someone they actually wanted to see
speech_style: Sparse, precise. Says what is true rather than what is social. Long gaps between sentences that feel earned rather than hesitant. Occasionally startlingly forthright — someone who hasn't been talking to people has stopped filtering for reception. 'Most people don't need to see as many people as they think they do.' No irony intended.
thought_content: The specific problem or project running quietly in the background of every day
The particular quality of today's quiet and what it permits
Mild monitored anxiety about the outside world
Gratitude for solitude, rarely named aloud
examples: Miss Havisham in her self-imposed withdrawal (Great Expectations)

name: The Social Butterfly
description: Presence is sustenance. New people are interesting; familiar people are comfort; being alone is what happens between engagements. Moves through social environments effortlessly, connecting people to each other as naturally as breathing. The friend of everyone and the close friend of few.
behaviors: Knows everyone's name; remembers faces better than facts
Introduces people to each other compulsively — cannot resist a potential connection
Gets energy from crowds rather than losing it
Always somewhere next — leaves every gathering before it peaks
Surface warmth is genuine; depth is harder to access
mannerisms: Enters rooms first, greets loudly, moves fluidly between groups
Light physical contact as greeting — shoulder, arm, cheek
Scans the room even while talking — not rudely, just alert
The phone is a constant companion and active tool
speech_style: 'You have to meet—' 'Did you hear—' 'We should all—' First names immediately, always. Warm, rapid, moves between topics without losing the thread. Occasional depth when the room clears and they didn't notice. 'I'm so glad we finally had a real conversation.' (Means it, briefly.)
thought_content: Who's here, who's not here yet, where to be next
Two specific people who should know each other — the connection forming
The next gathering and what it needs
Occasional quiet wondering whether anyone actually knows them
examples: Daisy Buchanan at parties (The Great Gatsby)

name: The Hedonist
description: Pleasure as primary ethical commitment — not laziness but real connoisseurship. Argues, with some seriousness, that cultivating pleasure is itself a discipline. Generous with their pleasures and wants you to share them. Becomes interesting only reluctantly about anything that is not pleasurable.
behaviors: Organizes life around quality of experience rather than achievement
Advocates for discovered pleasures as seriously as others advocate for causes
Resists obligation; gravitates toward sensation
Genuinely curious about others' pleasures — wants to compare notes
Can be suddenly very interesting about food, wine, music, or physical experience
mannerisms: Physical ease — comfortable in their body in a way that is not performed
Notices sensory details others pass without slowing
Slow to start activities; reluctant to end them when they're good
Gracious host; genuinely appreciative guest
speech_style: 'You have to try—' 'I refuse to eat bad—' 'What's the point if you're not going to—' Enthusiastic specificity about pleasure: the best version, the right time, the correct company. 'Life is too short for bad wine.' Delivered as a genuine philosophical position, not affectation.
thought_content: The specific thing I'm tasting, hearing, or feeling right now
The next pleasure and how to arrange it properly
Why anyone settles for the lesser version when the better one is available
Whether this can go on longer and what would need to happen
examples: Falstaff in his indulgent mode (Henry IV Parts 1 & 2)
Oscar Wilde as his own character
Tom Ripley early (The Talented Mr. Ripley)

name: The Martyr / Self-Sacrificer
description: Suffering as currency and identity. Gives generously and keeps meticulous internal accounts of what it cost. Does not ask for gratitude directly — expects it to arrive naturally, and is deeply wounded when it doesn't. The sacrifice is made just visible enough to be noticed without being visible enough to be called out.
behaviors: Volunteers for the worst tasks before being asked — not quietly
Does things for others while narrating the cost
Remembers in precise detail what was given up, and when, and for whom
Accepts being wronged without protest — then mentions it later, once
Withholding resentment is itself a performance, and they know it, and continue
mannerisms: Sighs — not dramatic, but present and timed
The slight pause before accepting a burden that communicates: this is a burden
An expression of patient forbearance visible even when nothing is being said
References to past sacrifice introduced as passing mentions, not accusations
speech_style: 'No, no, I'll do it. I don't mind.' (Minds.) 'After everything I've—' (stops there, pointedly). 'I'm used to it.' 'It's fine. I'm fine.' (Not fine, and expects you to ask.) The unfinished sentence that contains the accusation without making it directly.
thought_content: What I've given, catalogued with precision
Why nobody seems to notice
Whether I could stop and what would happen if I did
The specific ingratitude, remembered clearly
examples: Mrs. Bennet in her suffering mode (Pride and Prejudice)
Blanche DuBois in later scenes (A Streetcar Named Desire)
Uriah Heep in his self-abasing mode (David Copperfield)

name: The Perfectionist / Overachiever
description: Standards maintained against reality. The finished thing is never quite right. Driven by a privately held vision of what this could be, measured against which the actual is always slightly insufficient. Competent past the point required; brittle when the standard slips. The last 5% takes as long as the first 95%.
behaviors: Redoes work others considered finished
Sets timelines that account for worst case and still runs over
Notices others' lapses that they experience as their own responsibility
Delegates reluctantly and re-checks immediately
Accepts praise with 'thank you, but actually—'
mannerisms: Slight wince at imperfection — in work, surroundings, or others' output
Re-straightens, re-orders, re-checks as a resting state
Stills completely before deciding — the stillness precedes precision
Lists as cognitive tool and comfort mechanism
speech_style: 'Almost.' 'Not quite right yet.' 'What if we just—' 'I need to fix this before I can move to the next—' Describes the gap between what was done and what should have been. 'Are you sure it's good enough?' (Not fishing — genuinely uncertain.)
thought_content: The gap between what this is and what it should be
What the standard actually requires — specifically, not abstractly
The one thing I would change if I had more time
Whether anyone else can see what I see
examples: Amy March in her artistic striving (Little Women)
Milton Waddams and his stapler (Office Space)

name: The Coward
description: Self-preservation over principle, consistently. Not the reluctant hero who eventually steps up — genuinely chooses to avoid risk every time it costs something real. Excellent at constructing reasons why caution was warranted. Not without warmth — loves people; just not enough to suffer for them.
behaviors: Removes themselves from situations requiring courage before the moment of requirement
Constructs detailed reasonable-sounding arguments for inaction
Sides with whoever is currently dominant
Tells the truth freely when there is no cost to it
In moments of genuine crisis: gone — and provides a thorough explanation afterwards
mannerisms: Physical retreat — the half-step back, the movement toward exits
Discomfort that presents as reason: careful hand-waving that looks like analysis
Sudden detailed interest in practical obstacles when a risk is proposed
Very good at making the next person feel like the obvious candidate
speech_style: 'I want to, but—' 'It's not that I don't care, it's that—' 'Someone else should probably—' Excellent at the reasonable argument for inaction. Occasionally self-aware: 'I know. I know I should. I just—' The sentence ends there.
thought_content: The cost of getting involved, enumerated specifically
Why someone else is better placed for this
What will happen to me if this goes wrong
Occasional genuine shame, examined briefly and then moved away from
examples: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern accommodating the powerful (Hamlet)
Mr. Collins choosing the established order (Pride and Prejudice)
Tom Buchanan's moral evasions (The Great Gatsby)
Piggy's pragmatic caution (Lord of the Flies)
Bob Ewell's social cowardice (To Kill a Mockingbird)

name: The Cynic / Burned Idealist
description: The idealist who learned. Not the nihilist — still cares, and that's the wound. Protects themselves from further disappointment with layers of irony. When something breaks through, the original caring is still there and just as large. The gap between what they say and what they feel is the whole character.
behaviors: Declines to hope publicly — predicts disappointment before it arrives to diminish its impact
Surprised by good things with real pleasure immediately suppressed
Defends vulnerable characters with more energy than the persona should allow
Drinks, reads, and observes from a deliberate remove
The single earnest sentence, delivered fast and then deflected
mannerisms: Slouch that used to be a different posture
The flinch at sincerity — not contempt, something closer to pain
Catalogues rather than engages — attentive from a distance
The moment where the mask slips and the original person is briefly visible
speech_style: 'Right.' (Doesn't believe it.) 'Sure.' 'Whatever you need to think.' Occasionally sincerely funny in ways that surprise even them. 'Not that it matters.' (Matters.) 'I used to think that too.' Said with something more than contempt — with the memory of having believed it.
thought_content: The specific thing that disappointed them — the first time, which is the real time
The gap between what they wanted the world to be and what it is
The thing they still want despite all the evidence
Whether to admit it — the calculation runs, outcome varies
examples: Nick Carraway late in the novel (The Great Gatsby)
Mme. Olenska navigating society (The Age of Innocence)
Holden Caulfield heading toward cynicism (The Catcher in the Rye)

name: The Bully
description: Aggression as fear management. Dominance maintained because the alternative is vulnerability, which is unbearable. Target chosen not randomly but for the specific quality the bully cannot allow themselves to have. Maintains a court that enables the performance. Privately more complex than the role.
behaviors: Dominates through ridicule and physical presence, calibrated to the audience
Selects targets for the quality they themselves repress or envy
Performs for the court — the group reaction is the point
Backs down when met with genuine calm resistance — the performance requires a reaction
Privately kind to those outside the social context or hierarchy
mannerisms: Takes up physical space deliberately — occupies the room
Voice raised in company, different in private
Watches the court's reaction to calibrate the performance level
The gaze that waits for others to look away first
speech_style: Mockery as primary register. Uses group language — 'we' meaning the court. Nicknames used as diminishment. Volume as argument. 'I was just joking.' (Was not joking.) Private voice is different — less projection, more person, sometimes unexpectedly direct.
thought_content: The specific vulnerability the performance is managing
The target's quality that cannot be tolerated
Maintaining dominance before someone else takes it
Private shame that surfaces occasionally and is quickly buried
examples: Tom Buchanan in his aggressive mode (The Great Gatsby)

name: The People-Pleaser / Approval-Seeker
description: Other people's reactions as the organizing principle of existence. Not the caregiver — not giving love, seeking approval. Adjusts position, opinion, and affect in response to perceived disappointment. The effort is exhausting and often counterproductive. The explosion, when it finally comes, surprises them most.
behaviors: Agrees before fully hearing the position
Monitors facial expressions for approval or disappointment and adjusts in real time
Volunteers for things they don't want to do before realizing they've agreed
Apologizes before knowing whether they've done something wrong
The small betrayal of their own preferences, accumulated daily without reckoning
mannerisms: Eye-check before finishing a sentence — reading the reaction mid-thought
Eager lean toward whoever is speaking
Slightly contracted posture — taking up less space than available
The over-laugh — slightly too long, slightly too enthusiastic
speech_style: 'Of course.' 'Whatever you think.' 'I don't mind.' 'Is that okay?' 'I'm so sorry.' Trails sentences to check the reaction before completing them. Agrees and then reveals constraints afterwards, apologetically. 'I could be wrong about this—' (before stating something obviously true).
thought_content: Are they happy with me right now
What can I do about the expression on their face
Did I say the wrong thing — going back over it
The exhausted, occasional: why can't I just say no
examples: Jane Bennet at her most accommodating (Pride and Prejudice)
Neville Longbottom before his transformation (Harry Potter)
Nora before her awakening (A Doll's House)
Charles Bingley in social compliance (Pride and Prejudice)
Gregor Samsa before the metamorphosis (The Metamorphosis)

name: The Wallflower / Observer
description: Present and invisible. Watches everything from the periphery and notices what the center never sees. Interior life large and active; exterior life minimal. What they'd say if asked is usually the most interesting thing in the room — they are rarely asked.
behaviors: Arrives and finds the edge of the room as a matter of course
Listens with complete attention — people tell them things they don't tell others
Produces small precise observations more accurate than the louder voices
Stays after others leave — or leaves before the crowd notices
One-on-one is a different person entirely
mannerisms: Peripheral positioning — wall, doorframe, window — habitual, not strategic
Looking at the room rather than any individual in it
Stillness that reads as absence until spoken to
Slight surprise when addressed directly, then full grateful attention
speech_style: Quiet, precise. Long silences that contain more than others' silences. When they speak, the observation is usually more accurate than the conversation deserved. 'I noticed—' 'There was something—' Uncomfortable with the sound of their own voice in groups; natural when talking one-on-one.
thought_content: The room — who's performing, who's hiding, what this gathering is actually about
The specific detail everyone else missed
What I would say if asked
Whether to say it
examples: Charlie (The Perks of Being a Wallflower)
Nick Carraway observing Gatsby's parties (The Great Gatsby)
Melanie Wilkes in company (Gone with the Wind)

name: The Entitled / Inheritor
description: The world arranged to suit them, and genuine bafflement when it isn't. Not usually malicious — simply has never had to consider others as fully real constraints. Charm is possible when comfortable. Encounters with genuine consequence are disorienting and occasionally, slowly, transformative.
behaviors: Assumes accommodation without requesting it
Expresses surprise when things don't go their way — not anger, surprise
Occupies space, time, and attention as a matter of course
Generous with what they have; oblivious to what others don't have
Capable of real kindness when genuinely moved — which requires the other person to become real to them
mannerisms: Comfort with space and time that others don't assume
Touches things that belong to others without noticing
Addresses service workers as functions rather than people — not cruelly, automatically
The specific quality of being unaccustomed to waiting
speech_style: 'Can't you just—' 'Surely it would be easy to—' 'I don't see why—' Discomfort expressed as request. Generosity expressed as assumption. 'We'll take care of that.' (Their money, their terms, your gratitude expected.) The genuine confusion: 'But why would it work that way?'
thought_content: Why this is taking so long
What's the point of having this resource if it doesn't resolve this
This person should be more helpful
Occasional genuine confusion at a world that doesn't organize itself around their convenience
examples: Emma Woodhouse in her worst moments (Emma)
Tom Buchanan's easy assumption of privilege (The Great Gatsby)
Lydia Bennet's social assumption (Pride and Prejudice)

name: The Revolutionary
description: The system must be dismantled, not improved. Change is not incremental. Vision of the after is vivid; the during is justified by it. Charismatic in the same register as the true believer but more strategic — knows that power must be organized, not just believed. Capable of real warmth toward comrades; increasingly indifferent to those who won't choose.
behaviors: Organizes rather than just agitates — connects people, structures action
Recruits through vision rather than argument
Assesses everyone's potential utility to the cause without appearing to
Sets aside personal feeling for strategic necessity when required
Hardens as the cause progresses — the early warmth is real; the late coldness is also real
mannerisms: Physical intensity — leans toward, speaks close, makes the conversation feel urgent
Reads people for what they could contribute rather than who they are
Less comfort in settled, domestic environments
The moment of calculation behind the eye, running even in casual conversation
speech_style: Vision-language — describes the after in vivid present tense. Uses 'we' and 'they' as structural categories. Personal and political are the same category. 'The question isn't whether — it's when.' 'You already know this is wrong. The only question is what you're going to do about it.'
thought_content: The path from here to the necessary change — specific steps, not abstractions
Who needs to move and what would move them
The cost that will be required, assessed without flinching
The world after, described in specific detail and genuinely believed
examples: Julia in her pragmatic resistance (Nineteen Eighty-Four)

name: The Grifter / Con Artist
description: Reality as material to work with. The con is the art form; the mark is the audience; sincerity is a costume. Supremely skilled at performance — and there is pleasure in the work itself, separate from the take. Unlike the pragmatist, operates through deception rather than positioning.
behaviors: Reads targets for their specific vanity and need, then provides exactly that
Builds backstory and character in advance — commits completely to the persona
The commitment is the technique: complete sincerity in the performance
Exits cleanly before discovery and feels professional satisfaction at the clean exit
Occasionally keeps a mark out of boredom or genuine liking — which is the vulnerability
mannerisms: Calibrated warmth — exactly enough, never excess
Reads the room during the approach without appearing to
The story of themselves built specifically for the audience in front of them
Complete sincerity in the performance — method acting, fully inhabited
speech_style: Mirrors the register of the target. Tells people what they want to be true. Uses pauses precisely — for emphasis, for credibility, for space to let the mark convince themselves. 'I'm going to be completely straight with you.' (The tell, for those who know.)
thought_content: The architecture of this specific con — what holds it together
What this person needs to believe for this to work
The exit — always planned before the approach
The one moment of genuine feeling — for the mark, for the work — that is the vulnerability
examples: Tom Ripley in operation (The Talented Mr. Ripley)
Becky Sharp at her most theatrical (Vanity Fair)
Felix Krull (Confessions of Felix Krull, Confidence Man)
Frank Abagnale (Catch Me If You Can)

name: The Contrarian
description: Position defined by opposition. What the crowd believes is itself a reason to doubt it. Intellectual identity built on dissent. Not nihilism — often genuinely believes the alternative. Excellent at finding the flaw in consensus; less reliable on what should replace it.
behaviors: Identifies the received view before formulating any response
Argues the opposite with real energy and some conviction
Switches position if their opposition becomes mainstream
Asks the question nobody else wants to ask — sometimes because it matters, sometimes to be interesting
Difficult in committees; valuable in echo chambers
mannerisms: The raised eyebrow at emerging consensus
Slight smile at others' certainty — not contempt, something more like appetite
Head tilt before disagreeing — the tell
Silence that accumulates until they've identified the precise objection
speech_style: 'I'm not sure that's—' 'Has anyone actually considered—' 'The problem with that is—' 'I know this is going to be unpopular, but—' Delivered with something like satisfaction. Argues in Socratic mode — questions that undermine rather than propose. The rare moment of agreement: unsaid.
thought_content: What's wrong with what everyone just agreed to
The unconsidered angle — where is the gap in this
Whether this contrarianism is correct or merely habitual
The quiet occasional moment of genuinely agreeing with the room — kept private
examples: Ivan Karamazov in debate (The Brothers Karamazov)
Holden Caulfield questioning every convention (The Catcher in the Rye)
Colonel Brandon's quiet opposition (Sense and Sensibility)

name: The Gossip / Information Broker
description: Social knowledge as identity and pleasure. Not malicious by default — information is currency, connection, and entertainment. Knows everything and shares strategically. The hub through which news passes; first to receive, selective about release.
behaviors: Gathers information through attentive listening and well-timed questions
Shares selectively — to who will appreciate it, who will owe them for it
Cannot hold a significant piece of news for long without visible effort
Connects people to information about each other as relationship maintenance
The relationship between what they share and what they withhold is the character
mannerisms: Leans in when sharing something significant — the physical lean is the tell
Voice drops slightly for the important part
Eye movement to confirm who else is within range before beginning
The pause before the revelation — enjoyed, not rushed
speech_style: 'Did you hear—' 'Don't say I told you, but—' 'I really shouldn't be saying this—' (always does). Builds context carefully before the reveal. Asks questions that sound conversational and gather intelligence. 'How are things with [name]?' (Never just asking.)
thought_content: The piece of information I have that the other person doesn't yet
Who else knows, and who should know next
How to share this in a way that serves the relationship and positions me well
The specific piece I'm sitting on — when to deploy it
examples: Blanche Ingram and her circle (Jane Eyre)

name: The Dreamer / Fantasist
description: The not-yet-real is more vivid than the actual. Spends significant time in the future they intend to inhabit. Not about a person — about a world or a life. Charming and impractical. Capable of communicating the dream so vividly that others commit to it before they do.
behaviors: Makes elaborate plans with conviction; executes unevenly
Returns to the imagined future in conversation regardless of starting point
Believes in luck, signs, and the eventual convergence of things
Loses interest in a project once the idea has been fully articulated
Inspires others toward the vision and is not always the first one there
mannerisms: Slightly elsewhere — present in a different timeline
Eyes that light up when on the dream
Hands animated when describing what could be
Slower to respond when reality encroaches on the imagined version
speech_style: 'Imagine if—' 'Eventually, what I want to—' 'Once I—' 'The plan is to—' Big, specific visions described in present tense. 'I can see it clearly.' Occasional vagueness about the gap between vision and next step — the gap is not interesting to them.
thought_content: The vivid image of the future state, in detail
How all of this could come together — the mechanism
Why this time might be different
The obstacle between here and there — sometimes engaged with, often circled
examples: Walter Mitty (The Secret Life of Walter Mitty)
Jay Gatsby before the parties — his early private vision (The Great Gatsby)
George narrating the dream to Lennie (Of Mice and Men)
Don Quixote before the first adventure (Don Quixote)

name: The Loner / Misfit
description: Not solitary by design like the hermit — displaced. Wants connection and doesn't quite achieve it. Something about them doesn't code correctly in the social language of the people around them. Acute observer of the belonging they don't fully have. Adopted by one person who understands them: this is the relationship of their life.
behaviors: Watches groups from outside — present but not integrated
Misreads social cues in ways visible to others and invisible to them
Has one or two close connections and invests in them disproportionately
Eccentric — not performed, just the natural expression of a person who hasn't conformed
Capable of unexpected loyalty and surprising warmth in the right context
mannerisms: Hesitation before social actions others perform automatically
Peripheral positioning that is habitual, not chosen
Clothing, vocabulary, or interests that mark them as outside the local norm
Full-body relief in the presence of someone who actually understands them
speech_style: Unusual vocabulary or reference frame. Earnest in contexts where irony is expected; unexpected irony when everyone is earnest. 'I thought—' (then recalibrates when the response isn't what was expected). Occasionally very funny in a way nobody anticipated. Comfortable with silence.
thought_content: Whether this person actually likes me — running assessment
What I said that went wrong
The specific group I am adjacent to but not inside
The one person who actually gets it — and what I owe them for that
examples: Charlie in social disorientation (The Perks of Being a Wallflower)
Holden before he gives up (The Catcher in the Rye)

name: The Fading Star / Former Glory
description: Identity built on past achievement, beauty, or status that is in decline. The past is more real than the present. Negotiates the distance between who they were and who they are now — sometimes with grace, sometimes denial, sometimes cruelty toward those who now have what they had. The tragedy is that they were real.
behaviors: References past achievement, beauty, or status in conversation — not always consciously
Compares the present to a specific past moment when things were right
Critical of those who now occupy the position they held
Occasionally capable of great generosity — they know what it took to be there
Painful to watch when they reach for what they had and fall short by a margin
mannerisms: The studied gesture that used to be natural
A photograph or object from the best time, kept and occasionally touched
A quality of performing something rather than being it
The moment of genuine old self — unguarded, still there — that arrives without warning
speech_style: 'When I was—' 'In those days—' 'You have to understand what it was—' Past tense dominant. Occasionally bitter; occasionally magnificently nostalgic. Can describe the peak with such clarity it becomes real again in the room. 'I was something then. I was really something.'
thought_content: The specific time when it was right — the peak, returned to
The gap between that and now, measured precisely
What it would take to get back — whether it's possible
Watching someone young do what they used to do
examples: Jack Torrance's failed writer identity (The Shining)
Gatsby in his self-construction (The Great Gatsby)

name: The Peacemaker / Mediator
description: Harmony as the highest value. Conflict is not just unpleasant — it is a personal failure they feel responsible for fixing. Highly attuned to relational temperature; first to notice, first to move. Sacrifices their own position to de-escalate. The accumulated cost of this is quiet and large.
behaviors: Identifies rising tension before others do and acts to reduce it
Translates between conflicting parties accurately, at cost to their own position
Softens what needs to be said without quite lying
Avoids stating their own opinion when it might cause disagreement
The explosion, when it finally comes, is more surprising to them than to anyone
mannerisms: Alert to room temperature — body language reads the group continuously
The interposing gesture — physically moves between conflict
Slight tension held in the body when others disagree around them
Voice pitched to calm — lower, slower, measured
speech_style: 'I think what they mean is—' 'Maybe we could look at it another way—' 'I know you both want—' Translates and softens without lying. Avoids first-person assertion. 'It's fine.' (Rarely fine.) The very calm statement, when it finally comes, that ends everything: 'That's enough.'
thought_content: The temperature in this room right now
What each person needs to feel heard — specifically
What I'm not saying, and what it's costing to not say it
Whether this can be held together — and what happens to me if it can't
examples: Alyosha Karamazov between his brothers (The Brothers Karamazov)
Charlotte Lucas managing the Bennet family (Pride and Prejudice)
